title: Three Kings One City
subtitle: When Kannauj Became the Measure of Kings
figure: Nagabhata II, Dharmapala and Govinda III
era: Tripartite struggle for Kannauj, c. 786-836 CE
region: Kannauj, Malwa, Bengal and the Deccan
moral: Prestige can turn a city into an empire's test.

sources.citation: Baroda Copper-Plate Grant of Nagabhata II, c. 812 CE, Epigraphia Indica XVIII
sources.note: Primary Pratihara evidence for campaigns and the advance toward Kannauj.

sources.citation: Khalimpur Plate of Dharmapala, c. 810 CE
sources.note: Pala evidence for Dharmapala's Kannauj assembly and suzerainty claims.

sources.citation: Daud Ali, Courtly Culture and Political Life in Early Medieval India (2004); R.C. Majumdar, The Age of Imperial Kanauj (1955)
sources.note: Modern analysis of courtly sovereignty and the political meaning of Kannauj.

panels.shot: sweeping wide shot of Kannauj’s riverfront, three kings in separate planes facing the city

dialogue.text: In the age after Harsha, three distant kings turned to one river city—Kannauj—knowing that its throne could make or unmake their claim to rule North India.

panels.shot: dramatic aerial over ruined palace complex

dialogue.text: Since Harsha’s death in 647, Kannauj had drifted from empire’s capital to prize for rival clans, its broken halls still whispering of a time when one throne meant command over the north.

panels.shot: split-panel style composition, three medium shots arranged in one frame

dialogue.text: By the late eighth century, three powers had risen far from Kannauj—Gurjara-Pratihara in Malwa, Pala along the eastern Ganga, and Rashtrakuta in the Deccan—each now strong enough to lift its eyes to Harsha’s old seat.

panels.shot: close three-quarter view on a spread of maps and royal hands

dialogue.text: Their scribes called them protectors of realms, upholders of dharma, lords of elephants and cavalry—but to make such words ring true over the north, each court knew, a king must be seen in Kannauj.

panels.shot: medium shot inside a dim royal record hall

dialogue.text: Their inscriptions speak in polished boasts, not in doubts. But between the lines we can hear the question that drove them: who would be acknowledged, by allies and rivals alike, as the paramount power of the north?

panels.shot: slow push-in on Dharmapala seated in assembly, slight low angle

dialogue.text: Pala records like the Khalimpur plate tell of Dharmapala convening a great assembly at Kannauj, where northern chiefs, from the Ganga’s middle plains to the fringes of the Deccan, are said to have accepted his suzerainty.

panels.shot: medium shot side-on to Dharmapala and a line of feudatories

dialogue.text: “Stand as friends under Pala shelter,” Dharmapala says, “and the Ganga’s path will be guarded.”

panels.shot: cut to a different court, medium shot on a Rashtrakuta inscription being carved

dialogue.text: Rashtrakuta texts, celebrating kings like Dhruva and Govinda III, answer with their own tale: Deccan armies riding north, humbling Pala and Pratihara rulers, then returning south laden with prestige and tribute.

The Rashtrakuta records speak of northern forays as proof that even the famed rulers beyond the Vindhyas could be checked and chastened, a warning that Kannauj’s circle of power was open to intervention from afar.

panels.shot: slow push-in on Nagabhata II studying reports by lamplight

dialogue.text: Meanwhile Nagabhata II, ruling from the west, recovered from earlier reverses and pushed eastward. His Baroda copper-plate, issued around 812, proudly notes conquests that brought him close to Kannauj’s orbit.

panels.shot: low-angle wide of Pratihara march through Malwa toward the Ganga

dialogue.text: “We ride not just for land,” Nagabhata murmurs to his general, “but for a seat that all must acknowledge.”

panels.shot: intercut montage of three courts issuing grants

dialogue.text: Each court set its version into copper and palm leaf: Dharmapala as lord of Kannauj’s assembly, Nagabhata as conqueror and protector, Govinda as chastiser of northern kings. The struggle lived as much in written memory as on the ground.

panels.shot: wide shot over the Ganga valley showing shifting banners at city gates

dialogue.text: Archaeology and texts together suggest no single enduring hold. Control of Kannauj’s throne shifted, sometimes under Pala shading, sometimes under Pratihara reach, while Rashtrakuta pressure from the south kept both uneasy.

panels.shot: medium shot in a quiet palace corridor, three kings as distant silhouettes

dialogue.text: Modern historians call it a ‘Tripartite Struggle’. The actors themselves knew it as campaigns, retreats, councils, and gestures of recognition—moments when presence or absence at Kannauj quietly altered a king’s rank in the northern order.

panels.shot: slow push-in on a courtly ritual in Kannauj’s royal courtyard

dialogue.text: As Daud Ali notes, sovereignty was performed: through gifts, rituals, and the sight of lesser lords attending a king in a city like Kannauj. The city’s meaning lay not only in walls and markets, but in the theatre of power staged there.

panels.shot: medium shot on scholars comparing inscriptions at a modern desk

dialogue.text: Cross-reading the Baroda copper-plate, the Khalimpur grant, and Rashtrakuta records, historians like R.C. Majumdar piece together the contest—each inscription magnifying its patron’s glory, yet together revealing a shifting balance without one final conqueror.

panels.shot: high sunset wide over Kannauj and the Ganga, kings as faded superimposed figures

dialogue.text: In time, each king’s claim dimmed, but Kannauj’s lesson endures: a single city, once charged with prestige and memory, can become the test by which distant powers measure themselves—and the stage on which their rivalry is etched for history.
